readerTitle: Why your first fans can't get you to the mainstream
caseNote: 실제 연구·이론 (Rogers의 혁신 확산 모델, Moore의 캐즘 이론) + 가상 사례 두 개 (식물성 치즈 제조사, 치과용 예약 소프트웨어)
insight: 초기 성공이 멈추는 이유는 제품이 아니라 구매자가 바뀌었기 때문이다. 새로움을 사는 사람과 안전함을 사는 사람은 다른 제안이 필요하다.
misconception: 초기 고객이 열광하면 그 열기가 자연스럽게 일반 고객에게 번진다. 성장이 멈추면 더 많은 화제와 홍보가 필요하다.

sources.text: Moore, G. A. (1991). Crossing the Chasm. HarperBusiness.
Rogers, E. M. (1962). Diffusion of Innovations. Free Press. (채택자 분류와 비율 2.5/13.5/34/34/16%)
치즈 제조사와 예약 소프트웨어 사례 및 수치(병원 40곳 등)는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Rogers의 채택자 분류 비율(혁신자 2.5%, 초기 수용자 13.5%, 초기 다수 34%, 후기 다수 34%, 지각 수용자 16%)은 정규분포를 가정한 이상화된 모델입니다. 합계 100% 확인. 카드에도 실제 측정치가 아니라 모델이라고 적었습니다.
Moore의 책 초판 연도(1991)와 용어(visionaries, pragmatists, whole product), 그리고 캐즘이 초기 수용자와 초기 다수 사이에 있다는 주장을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.
Moore가 주로 하이테크 B2B 시장을 다뤘다는 7번 카드의 설명이 정확한지 확인이 필요합니다.
Rogers 초판 출간 연도(1962)와 Rogers를 'sociologist'로 표기해도 되는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why your first fans can't get you to the mainstream
body: Two young businesses: a plant-based cheese maker and a scheduling app for dental clinics.
Both had a brilliant first year, with fans, buzz and fast growth. Both stalled in year two. The products hadn't changed. The buyers had.

image.label: Two rising sales lines that both flatten at the same point
image.brief: 두 개의 성장 그래프를 나란히 배치. 왼쪽은 치즈 조각 아이콘, 오른쪽은 달력 앱 아이콘. 두 선 모두 빠르게 오르다가 같은 지점에서 평평해지고, 그 앞에 얕은 골짜기(틈)가 보이도록. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The chefs love it. The pizzerias say "maybe later."
body: Mara's plant-based cheese sells out to adventurous chefs and food fans. They love trying new things and forgive the odd batch that melts badly.
Now she pitches ordinary pizzerias and family restaurants. They taste it, smile and say "maybe later." What should she do?

options.text: Launch three bold new flavors to recreate the early buzz
options.feedback: Novelty is what her first fans wanted. Busy restaurant owners aren't asking for something new. They're asking whether it's safe.

options.text: Win over one ordinary pizzeria completely: steady supply, tested in their ovens, a clear cost per pizza. Then use it as proof
options.feedback: Slower and less exciting, but it answers what a cautious owner really asks: does this work for a place like mine?

options.text: Cut the price 30% so trying it costs less
options.feedback: A lower price removes one risk. But the owner's bigger fear is a bad pizza on a busy Friday night, and price doesn't fix that.

cards.title: Same wall, different industry.
body: Dev's scheduling app took off with tech-minded dentists. They signed up after one demo, put up with bugs and built their own workarounds. They liked being first.
Then Dev called on regular clinics. Office managers asked: Does it connect to our billing system? Who trains my staff? Which clinic like ours uses it?
He had no good answers. Sales stalled at about 40 clinics.

image.label: An excited early user next to a cautious office manager with a checklist
image.brief: 왼쪽에는 새 기기를 들고 신난 치과의사, 오른쪽에는 체크리스트("Billing?", "Training?", "Who else?")를 든 신중한 병원 사무장. 두 사람 사이에 작은 틈. 실제 소프트웨어 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Buyers don't arrive as one crowd.
body: Everett Rogers sorted people by how early they adopt something new. These shares come from his idealized model, not from measuring any one market.

groups.label: Share of eventual buyers, by when they adopt

cards.callout: The trouble sits between the two highlighted groups: the first 16% and the big middle.

image.label: Adoption curve with the chasm
image.brief: Rogers groups with a labeled gap between early adopters and early majority.

cards.title: Crossing the chasm
body: In his 1991 book *Crossing the Chasm*, consultant Geoffrey Moore argued that the hardest step isn't the first sale. It's the jump from **early adopters** to the **early majority**.

Early adopters buy a chance to get ahead, so they accept rough edges. The early majority buys proven help with today's problem. They don't trust an adventurous fan's word, because that fan isn't like them.
So early success can stall right where the big market begins. That gap is the **chasm**.

image.label: A bridge being built across a gap between two groups of buyers
image.brief: 왼쪽 절벽 위에 소수의 모험적인 고객("Early adopters"), 오른쪽 넓은 땅에 많은 신중한 고객("Early majority"). 그 사이 협곡에 좁은 다리를 한 칸씩 놓는 장면. 다리 첫 칸에 "one customer like them" 라벨.

cards.title: Cautious buyers need a different offer, not a louder one.
body: Here is what the early majority looks for before saying yes:
list: **Proof from peers:** a customer like them, not a famous early fan
**A complete solution:** supply, setup, training and support, not just the core product
**Low risk:** consistency matters more than novelty
**Fit with what they already use:** their ovens, billing systems and routines
cards.callout: That's why crossing usually starts small: win one narrow group completely, so they can vouch for you to the next.

cards.title: Not every stall is a chasm.
body: Moore wrote mainly about technology sold to businesses. Many products never show a sharp gap, and some cheap consumer goods spread smoothly by word of mouth. The adoption percentages are a tidy model, not a law.
Also check who stopped buying. If cautious buyers hesitate but early fans keep reordering, you may face a chasm. If your early fans drift away too, the problem is probably the product.

cards.title: Back to Dev's app.
body: Dev has 40 enthusiastic clinics and a long list of curious but hesitant ones. Where should his next six months go?

options.text: Build the advanced features his early dentists keep requesting
options.feedback: It keeps loyal users happy, but they want extras. The mainstream is blocked on basics like billing links and staff training.

options.text: Pick one type of clinic, such as small family practices, and make the app complete for them: billing link, staff training and two clinics willing to take reference calls
options.feedback: He grows slower for a while, but each new clinic gets the proof and support a cautious buyer needs, and becomes a reference for the next.

options.text: Hire a sales team to call every clinic in the country
options.feedback: More calls run into the same unanswered questions. A bigger team just hears "maybe later" faster, at a higher cost.

cards.title: Your first fans and your next customers want different things.
body: Early buyers want what's new. Mainstream buyers want something safe, complete and proven by someone like them.
**Try it today:** list your last ten customers and mark each one *adventurous* or *cautious*. If they're all adventurous, write down what a cautious buyer would need before saying yes.
